items.title: Janis Siegel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 2015
items.q: And we did a whole record of vocalese with Jon and tackled some very meaty things.

ctx.x: No, I mean what was done with the vocals. Do you think it’s one of Manhattan Transfer’s best moments.

Yes. Absolutely. I think “Vocalese” is something that we’re very proud of, continuing the tradition of. And we did a whole record of vocalese with Jon and tackled some very meaty things. And Jon was able to tackle some meaty subjects in his lyrics, particularly “Joy Spring,” “Airegin” really amazing lyrics. And he was in the video of “Rock House” and he was in the video of “Night in Tunisia.” And whenever we could perform with Jon it’s always a blessing.
How is he doing these days?

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: My name is Tim Hauser and my girlfriend Janis Siegel and I live in Brooklyn and we’re going to start a Lambert, Hendricks & Ross type group called Manhattan Transfer.

ctx.x: And then I tell them the story of the formation of the Manhattan Transfer. Their idea was to be a group like Lambert, Hendricks & Ross. That’s why I helped them. That was their aim. I met Tim Hauser in a taxi. He was a taxi driver. And I got in his cab with my brother. And he says, “I know you, you’re Jon Hendricks.” I said, “how do you know me?” He says, “I know you. My name is Tim Hauser and my girlfriend Janis Siegel and I live in Brooklyn and we’re going to start a Lambert, Hendricks & Ross type group called…
Yeah, right. You summed it up. That’s great.

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: not only Tim’s, but Janice’s solo that she did.

ctx.x: Yeah. The tour wasn’t as long, because there were things that were left uncorrected that I heard about later. I always hear about solos that I write words to. Usually, if I’ve sung them, I usually get a great congratulations from the guy whose solo I sang. But up at the North Sea Jazz Festival, after the Manhattan Transfer album came out, Lee Konitz, whom I’ve known 40 years, was very angry at me. I gave him a big hug. He was like a little pouting kid.
